title: Works on My QPU: Reproducibility in Quantum Computing Research
authors: Dominik Köster, Maja Franz, Benjamin Zec, Nicole Hoess, Ralf Ramsauer, Wolfgang Mauerer
abstract: Quantum computing research increasingly depends on complex software stacks, yet the reproducibility of published results does not receive the priority and longevity mandated by recommendations of large international scientific bodies and best practices in software-centric systems research. In this paper, we present a combined manual and automated large-scale analysis of the reproducibility landscape in quantum computing research, quantify shortcomings, and derive actionable steps forward.   We manually evaluate a curated sample of 127 papers using a five-question framework that covers code availability, environment specification, documentation, hardware description, and executability. To place these findings in a broader context, we conduct an automated large-scale screening of nearly 5000 quantum computing papers for the same reproducibility indicators. Our manual analysis reveals that only 24.4% of the sampled papers provide code artefacts, and among those, 64.5% fail to execute successfully in a clean environment. This assessment is corroborated by a large-scale automated analysis that yields a consistent code availability rate of 26.8%. Further, it shows that approximately one-third of the papers with accessible code lack machine-readable environment specifications.   The results in this paper indicate that reproducibility is not yet consistently achieved in quantum computing research. In response, we outline a set of practical recommendations that address the observed failure modes and illustrate how reproducibility can be improved in practice.
summary: This paper analyzes the reproducibility crisis in quantum computing research by systematically auditing thousands of published papers. It finds that code artifacts are scarce and often fail to run due to incomplete environment specifications, rather than just missing code. The authors recommend adopting declarative tools to enforce rigorous, reproducible computational environments.
main_problem: The reproducibility of published results in quantum computing research is severely compromised by complex, evolving software stacks.
main_result: Reproducibility is not consistently achieved; only a small fraction of papers provide executable code artifacts with complete environment specifications.
method: The authors conducted a combined manual and automated large-scale analysis across thousands of QC papers using a five-criterion framework (code availability, environment specification, etc.).
model_or_system: The focus is on the software workflow surrounding quantum computing algorithms, which involve logical schedules transpiled to physical QPU circuits.
key_observables: Code availability rate (~25%), execution success rate among available code (low), and completeness of machine-readable environment specifications.
important_parameters: The analysis uses a five-question framework: Code Availability, Environment Specification, Documentation, Hardware Description, and Executability.
main_assumptions: The study assumes that reproducibility requires capturing the full execution context, necessitating declarative environment specification tools like Nix.
figures_summary: Figure 1 details the pipeline from a large initial corpus (4966 papers) down to the final set of manually validated NISQ-era papers (127).
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the problem, presents the methodology involving both manual and automated screening against five criteria, quantifies the failure rates across these metrics, and concludes with practical recommendations for improvement.
why_interesting: While focused on software best practices rather than physical Hamiltonians, the discussion of complex dependency management and required environmental rigor is highly relevant to simulating or analyzing open quantum systems that rely on specific numerical libraries.
analysis_basis: full PDF text, analyzed in chunks
